definition: A simple sort that repeatedly walks the array and swaps neighbouring elements that are out of order, so large values 'bubble' to the end. It is stable and in-place but makes O(n²) comparisons and swaps on average.
example: Sorting [3, 1, 2] takes two swaps: 3↔1, then 3↔2.

definition: A bubble sort variant that alternates left-to-right and right-to-left passes, so small elements near the end ('turtles') also move quickly. It is still O(n²) in the worst and average case.
example: It fixes [2, 3, 4, 5, 1] in two passes, where plain bubble sort needs four plus a check.

definition: Nicknames for elements in bubble sort: a large element near the start (a rabbit) races to the end in one pass, while a small element near the end (a turtle) moves only one place left per pass, which is what makes bubble sort slow.
example: In [2, 3, 4, 5, 1], the 1 is a turtle and needs four passes to reach the front.

definition: A pair of positions in an array where the earlier element is larger than the later one: a measure of how unsorted the array is. A sorted array has none; a reversed array of n distinct items has n(n−1)/2.
example: [3, 1, 2] has two inversions: (3, 1) and (3, 2).

definition: A sorting algorithm that runs faster when its input already has some order, such as few inversions or long sorted runs. Insertion sort and Timsort are adaptive; plain merge sort, selection sort and heapsort are not.
example: Timsort sorts an already sorted list of a million items with about a million comparisons instead of about 20 million.

definition: An algorithm that can process its input piece by piece as it arrives, without seeing it all first. Insertion sort is online: after each new element the prefix seen so far is sorted.
example: Inserting readings from a sensor into a sorted list one by one, as they arrive, is online sorting.

definition: Exchanging the contents of two positions in an array. Sorts are often compared by how many swaps (or other writes) they make, as well as how many comparisons, because writes can be expensive.
example: Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps; bubble sort makes one per inversion.

definition: In insertion sort, moving an element one place to the right to make room for the key being inserted. Each shift removes exactly one inversion.
example: Inserting 1 into the sorted prefix [2, 4, 5, 6] takes four shifts.

definition: A generalisation of insertion sort that first sorts elements far apart (a large gap), then progressively smaller gaps, ending with an ordinary insertion sort (gap 1). Long early moves remove many inversions at once. Its running time depends on the gap sequence.
example: A common gap sequence starts 701, 301, 132, 57, 23, 10, 4, 1 (Ciura's sequence).

definition: An ordering of n items chosen so that every one of the n! possible orderings is equally likely. Average-case results for sorts, such as about n(n−1)/4 inversions, assume this kind of input.
example: A properly shuffled deck of cards is a uniformly random permutation of 52 cards.

definition: Keys that are all different from one another, with no duplicates. Many sorting and selection results, such as randomised quicksort's 1.39 n log₂ n expected comparisons, are stated for distinct keys; duplicates can change the behaviour.
example: [3, 1, 2] has distinct keys; [2, 2, 1] does not.

definition: The value a sort orders records by. Records with equal keys are 'ties'; whether their original order survives depends on whether the sort is stable.
example: Sorting orders by delivery date makes the date the key; two orders on the same date have equal keys.

definition: The recursive form of merge sort: split the array in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the halves. It always does about n log₂ n work and needs an O(n) buffer for arrays.
example: Sorting 8 elements recurses down to 8 single elements, then merges back up in 3 levels.

definition: An iterative merge sort that treats the array as runs of length 1, merges neighbouring pairs into runs of 2, then 4, 8 and so on, with no recursion. It has the same O(n log n) cost and simple sequential passes.
example: An 8-element array is sorted in three passes: widths 1, 2 and 4.

definition: Extra memory an algorithm uses alongside its input to hold intermediate results. Array merge sort writes merged output into a buffer as large as the input, which is its main memory cost.
example: Merge-sorting 10 million 8-byte integers needs an 80 MB buffer.

definition: The first phase of external merge sort: read as much data as fits in memory, sort it, and write it to disk as a sorted run; repeat until all data is processed.
example: Sorting a 200 GB file in 4 GB chunks generates 50 runs.

definition: Merging k sorted sequences at once by repeatedly outputting the smallest of their k front elements, usually found with a min-heap of size k at O(log k) per element.
example: Merging 100 sorted runs uses a 100-element min-heap.

definition: A measure of how different two rankings are: the number of pairs of items they put in opposite orders. It equals the number of inversions between them and can be counted in O(n log n) with merge sort.
example: Rankings (A, B, C) and (B, A, C) have Kendall tau distance 1.

definition: A PostgreSQL setting for how much memory a single sort or hash operation may use before spilling to temporary files on disk. The default is 4 MB.
example: A sort needing 900 MB with work_mem at 4 MB runs as an external merge on disk.

definition: When an operation such as a sort runs out of its memory allowance and writes intermediate data to temporary files on disk, which is much slower than staying in memory.
example: PostgreSQL reports a spilled sort as 'Sort Method: external merge  Disk: ...'.

definition: A classic bug where computing a midpoint as (lo + hi) / 2 overflows a fixed-width integer when lo + hi exceeds its maximum, giving a negative index. The safe form is lo + (hi − lo) / 2.
example: With 32-bit ints, lo = 1.2 billion and hi = 1.4 billion sum to more than 2,147,483,647.

definition: An integer type with a set number of bits, such as 32 or 64, and therefore a largest and smallest value. Arithmetic past those limits overflows. Java's int and C's int32_t are fixed-width; Python's int is not.
example: A 32-bit signed integer holds −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647.

definition: Reading or writing data in order, one position after the next. Disks, caches and prefetchers handle it far better than random jumps, which is why merge-based external sorting and quicksort's partition scans are fast.
example: Merging 100 runs reads each run front to back: sequential access.

definition: Part of a CPU that spots regular memory access patterns, such as reading an array in order, and loads the next data into cache before it is asked for. It makes sequential scans fast and helps little with scattered jumps such as a heap's sift-down.
example: Quicksort's partition scan reads memory in order, so the prefetcher keeps the next cache lines ready.

definition: A programming model for processing large data sets across many machines: a map phase transforms records into key–value pairs, the pairs are sorted and grouped by key, and a reduce phase combines each group. Sorting map output is done with spill files and merges.
example: Counting words across terabytes of text is the classic MapReduce example.

definition: An embedded key–value storage engine from Meta based on an LSM tree. It writes sorted files and periodically merges them (compaction), a form of merge sort.
example: Many databases use RocksDB as their on-disk storage layer.

definition: Rearranging an array around a chosen pivot so that smaller elements come before larger ones. It is quicksort's core step and takes linear time; Lomuto and Hoare are the two classic schemes.

A simple quicksort partition that uses the last element as pivot and keeps a boundary of smaller elements at the front, then swaps the pivot into its final sorted position. It does more swaps than Hoare's scheme and is quadratic on all-equal keys.
example: On [7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4] with pivot 4, Lomuto ends with 4 at index 3.

definition: Tony Hoare's original 1961 partition: two indices move towards each other from the ends, swapping pairs that are on the wrong side. It does fewer swaps than Lomuto and balances all-equal keys, but does not leave the pivot in its final place.
example: Recursion after a Hoare partition uses [lo, p] and [p + 1, hi], not p − 1.

definition: The index an element will occupy once the whole array is sorted. Lomuto partition and quickselect rely on the pivot landing there, so it never needs to move again.
example: After partitioning around 4, the 4 at index 3 is already in its final sorted position.

definition: A pivot-selection rule: take the median of three medians, each of three sampled elements (nine elements in all). It gives better pivots than median-of-three on large arrays at small cost.
example: pdqsort uses the ninther for arrays above a size threshold.

definition: An input constructed, by someone who knows a quicksort's deterministic pivot rule, to make every partition lopsided and force quadratic time. Douglas McIlroy described a general method in 1999.
example: A median-of-3 killer sequence forces Θ(n²) on a median-of-three quicksort.

definition: The C standard library's general-purpose sort function. The standard specifies neither the algorithm nor stability, so behaviour differs between implementations.
example: qsort(arr, n, sizeof(int), cmp) sorts n ints with comparator cmp.

definition: A quicksort technique: recurse only into the smaller partition and handle the larger one with a loop. Each recursive call gets at most half the elements, so the stack depth is at most about log₂ n.
example: For a million elements the stack stays at most about 20 frames deep.

definition: Partitioning into three groups, less than, equal to and greater than the pivot, and recursing only on the outer two. It makes quicksort fast on inputs with many duplicates; all-equal keys take one linear pass.
example: Sorting a million orders by a five-value status field is a job for 3-way partitioning.

definition: Edsger Dijkstra's problem of arranging items of three colours so all of each colour are together, in one pass. Its solution is the basis of 3-way partitioning in quicksort.
example: Arranging [2, 0, 2, 1, 2, 0] around pivot 2 gives [0, 1, 0, 2, 2, 2].

definition: A quicksort variant by Vladimir Yaroslavskiy (2009) that uses two pivots to split the array into three parts. Java has used it for Arrays.sort on primitive arrays since Java 7.
example: Arrays.sort(int[]) in Java uses dual-pivot quicksort.

definition: The 2011 revision of the C++ language standard. Among many changes, it required std::sort to be O(n log n) in the worst case rather than only on average.
example: Code compiled with -std=c++11 or later gets the worst-case guarantee.

definition: Microsoft's software platform and runtime for languages such as C#. Its Array.Sort uses introsort.
example: Array.Sort(numbers) sorts a C# array in place with introsort.

definition: The textbook Introduction to Algorithms by Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, named from the authors' initials. It popularised the Lomuto partition in its quicksort chapter.
example: Many university algorithms courses use CLRS as the main text.

definition: Jon Bentley's classic book of essays on program design and algorithms (1986, 2nd edition 1999). It popularised the Lomuto partition and discussed binary search bugs.
example: Its binary search contained the midpoint overflow bug found in 2006.

definition: An attack that makes a service unavailable by exhausting a resource such as CPU time. Inputs that trigger worst-case algorithm behaviour, such as quadratic quicksort, are one way to do it.
example: A few crafted 10⁶-element arrays forcing 5 × 10¹¹ comparisons can tie up a server.

definition: A node in a tree that has at least one child. In a decision tree for sorting, each internal node is a comparison.
example: A full binary tree with 1,024 leaves has 1,023 internal nodes.

definition: A tree in which every node has at most two children. Heaps and decision trees for comparison sorts are binary trees.
example: A complete binary tree with 7 nodes has height 2.

definition: A way to model any comparison sort as a binary tree: each internal node is a comparison, each branch an answer, and each leaf a final ordering. The longest path is the worst-case number of comparisons, which proves the Ω(n log n) lower bound.
example: Sorting three elements needs a decision tree with at least 3! = 6 leaves and height at least 3.

definition: The theorem that any sort which learns about the input only by comparing pairs needs at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44n comparisons in the worst case (and on average), which is Ω(n log n).
example: Sorting a million distinct keys needs at least about 18.5 million comparisons.

definition: Describes an algorithm whose growth rate matches the proven lower bound for its problem, so no algorithm can beat it by more than a constant factor for large inputs. Merge sort and heapsort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts.
example: Merge sort's worst case for a million elements is about 18.95 million comparisons, within about 3% of the 18.49 million minimum.

definition: A comparison sort (1959), also called merge insertion, designed to use very few comparisons. It meets the lower bound for small inputs, such as 7 comparisons for 5 elements, but is impractical as a general sort.
example: Plain merge sort needs 8 comparisons for 5 elements; Ford–Johnson needs 7.

definition: Showing one problem is at least as hard as another by using a solution to the first to solve the second. If a fast priority queue would let you sort faster than the lower bound, that fast priority queue cannot exist.
example: Sorting reduces to building a BST and reading it in order.

definition: The priority-queue operation that removes and returns the smallest (or, for extract-max, largest) element. In a binary heap it costs O(log n): swap the root with the last element, shrink the heap and sift down.
example: Heapsort performs n − 1 extract-max operations.

definition: A way of merging two sequences into one while keeping each sequence's own order. Two sorted lists of sizes a and b can be merged in C(a + b, a) different ways.
example: Two lists of 3 can interleave in 20 ways.

definition: C(n, k), read 'n choose k': the number of ways to pick k items from n, equal to n! / (k! × (n − k)!).
Notation for n factorial, n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1: the number of different orderings of n distinct items.
example: 4! = 24, so there are 24 orderings of four distinct elements.

definition: The Linux kernel's general sorting routine, a heapsort: no recursion, no memory allocation and no worst-case input to exploit.
example: Kernel code sorts small tables with sort() from lib/sort.c.

definition: A system that must respond within guaranteed time limits. It favours algorithms with fixed worst-case bounds, such as heapsort, over ones that are faster on average.
example: An anti-lock braking controller is a real-time system.

definition: A slower but guaranteed algorithm that a hybrid switches to when its fast path goes badly, such as introsort switching from quicksort to heapsort when recursion gets too deep.
example: Introselect can fall back to median of medians to guarantee linear time.

definition: A non-comparison sort for integer keys in a small range 0..k−1: count each key, turn the counts into prefix sums to find where each key's block starts, then place each record. It costs O(n + k) time and space and can be stable.
example: Sorting 2 million exam scores from 0 to 100 needs just 101 counters.

definition: A non-comparison sort that breaks keys into digits and sorts one digit at a time with a stable counting sort. With d digits in base b it costs O(d × (n + b)).
example: 32-bit integers sort in 4 passes of one byte each.

definition: Least significant digit radix sort: sorts by the last (lowest) digit first and works towards the most significant, with a stable pass each time. Stability is what keeps earlier digits' order on ties.
example: Sorting [170, 45, 75] in base 10 sorts the ones digit, then tens, then hundreds.

definition: Most significant digit radix sort: splits keys into buckets by their first digit or character and recurses into each bucket. It suits variable-length strings because it stops once a bucket has one key.
example: Sorting words by first letter, then second letter within each bucket, is MSD radix sort.

definition: One piece of a key that radix sort sorts on at a time: a decimal digit, a byte, or a character. The number of digits per key sets the number of passes.
example: A 32-bit key has four 8-bit digits.

definition: The number of distinct values one digit can take. A larger base means fewer passes but a bigger count table per pass.
example: Base 256 uses one byte per digit and a 256-entry count table.

definition: In counting sort, k is the number of possible key values. Counting sort costs O(n + k), so it is only practical when k is not much larger than n.
example: Ages 0 to 130 give k = 131.

definition: The array of counters counting sort uses, one per possible key value; prefix sums over it give where each key's block starts in the output.
example: Base-256 radix sort uses a 256-entry count table per pass.

definition: The smallest and fastest level of CPU cache, typically tens of kilobytes per core. Data structures that fit in it, such as a 256-entry count table, are accessed very quickly.
example: A 65,536-entry count table no longer fits in a typical L1 cache.

definition: The second level of CPU cache, larger and slower than L1, typically hundreds of kilobytes to a few megabytes per core.
example: Base-2¹⁶ radix tables often live in L2 rather than L1.

definition: The most significant bit of a signed integer or floating-point number, set to 1 for negative values. Radix-sorting signed numbers requires flipping it so negatives come first.
example: XOR with 0x80000000 flips the sign bit of a 32-bit integer.

definition: Exclusive OR: a bitwise operation whose result bit is 1 when exactly one of the two input bits is 1. XOR with a mask flips exactly the bits set in the mask.
example: 5 XOR 3 = 6, because 101 XOR 011 = 110.

definition: The standard for floating-point arithmetic used by almost all hardware. It defines formats such as binary64 (Python's float, Java's double), special values like NaN and ±0.0, and comparison rules.
example: Positive IEEE 754 floats compare in the same order as their bit patterns read as unsigned integers.

definition: IEEE 754 has two zeros, +0.0 and −0.0, which compare equal but have different bit patterns, so a bit-based sort must decide whether to treat them as the same.
example: −0.0 == 0.0 is True in Python, but their bits differ in the sign bit.

definition: A number stored in binary scientific notation (sign, exponent and fraction), able to represent fractions and very large or small values approximately. Python's float is IEEE 754 binary64.
example: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004 because 0.1 has no exact binary representation.

definition: An integer type with no sign, holding only zero and positive values; a 32-bit unsigned integer holds 0 to 4,294,967,295.
example: Radix sort treats keys as unsigned integers so byte order matches numeric order.

definition: An unsigned 16-bit integer type, holding values 0 to 65,535.
example: A sensor reading stored as uint16 has only 65,536 possible values, ideal for counting sort.

definition: Spread evenly over a range, so every equal-width slice is equally likely to contain a value. Bucket sort's expected O(n) time assumes this.
example: Values from random.random() are uniformly distributed over [0, 1).

definition: The long-run average of a random quantity over all possible random outcomes. An 'expected O(n)' algorithm averages linear time, though an unlucky run can take longer.
example: Randomised quickselect makes about 3.4n expected comparisons to find a median.

definition: A generalisation of bucket sort that picks bucket boundaries from a random sample of the data, so buckets come out roughly equal even when the data is skewed. Distributed sorts use it to split data across machines.
example: TeraSort samples keys to choose the split points between machines.

definition: A count of how many values fall into each of a set of bins. In radix sorting, the histogram of digit values is the counting step that each pass starts with.
example: A base-256 radix pass builds a 256-bin histogram.

definition: In parallel computing, a scan computes all running totals of a list. Radix sort uses it to turn digit counts into output offsets; well-known parallel algorithms make it fast on GPUs.
example: The inclusive scan of counts [2, 0, 2, 3] is [2, 2, 4, 7]; the exclusive scan is [0, 2, 2, 4].

definition: A parallel operation that writes each element to a computed position in an output array. In radix sort each element is scattered to its slot after the prefix sum.
example: After the scan, every GPU thread scatters its elements to their output positions.

definition: Doing the same operation on many data items at once, across many processor cores or GPU threads. Counting, scans and scatters are data-parallel; comparison-heavy branching is less so.
example: A GPU can count digit values for millions of keys simultaneously.

definition: NVIDIA's CUDA library of reusable GPU primitives, including a fast radix sort built from histogram, scan and scatter passes.
example: cub::DeviceRadixSort sorts keys on an NVIDIA GPU.

definition: A company that designs GPUs and the CUDA platform for general-purpose computing on them.
example: CUB is NVIDIA's library of GPU building blocks.

definition: A benchmark and algorithm for sorting very large data sets (originally a terabyte) on a cluster with MapReduce. It samples keys to choose split points so each machine gets an even share.
example: Hadoop ships a TeraSort example job.

definition: NumPy's description of the type of the elements in an array, such as int64 or float32. np.sort chooses its algorithm partly by dtype.
example: np.array([1, 2]).dtype is int64 on most platforms.

definition: NumPy's sort function. kind='stable' uses radix sort for integer types of 16 bits or less and Timsort for other types (including 32- and 64-bit integers); the default kind='quicksort' is actually introsort.
example: np.sort(a, kind='stable') keeps equal elements in order.

definition: International Components for Unicode: a widely used library for Unicode text handling, including locale-aware collation. It can turn strings into byte sequences (collation keys) that sort correctly with plain byte comparison.
example: ICU's collation keys let names be sorted correctly for a German locale.

definition: A sort key made of several fields compared in order: the first field decides, and later fields break ties.
example: Sort by (last name, first name, date): ties on last name are broken by first name.

definition: A unit of 2³⁰ = 1,073,741,824 bytes, slightly more than a gigabyte (10⁹ bytes).
example: 16 GiB is about 17.2 GB.

definition: A unit of 10¹² bytes, a thousand gigabytes.
example: TeraSort was named after sorting a terabyte of data.

definition: The three-digit number a web server returns to say how a request went, such as 200 (OK) or 404 (Not Found). They fall in a small range, so counting sort fits them.
example: Sorting a day's request log by status code needs only a few hundred counters.

definition: A 32-bit number identifying a device on an IPv4 network, usually written as four bytes like 192.168.0.1. As 32-bit integers, they radix-sort in four byte passes.
A database designed for scanning and aggregating large amounts of data, often storing data by column. Some radix-sort encoded fixed-width keys instead of calling a comparator per pair.
example: DuckDB is an analytic engine.

definition: A byte encoding of a (possibly multi-field) key designed so that comparing the bytes gives the same order as comparing the original values, which lets radix sort or memcmp be used.
example: Encoding a signed int by flipping its sign bit and writing it big-endian makes a normalised key.

definition: Pattern-defeating quicksort, by Orson Peters (2016): an introsort descendant that adds pattern detection, equal-key partitioning, shuffles on bad partitions and branchless partitioning. It is unstable, in place, O(n log n) in the worst case, and linear on sorted, reversed and all-equal inputs. Go's sort.Sort uses it.
example: pdqsort sorts an already sorted array in O(n) via partial insertion sort.

definition: The unstable sort Rust has used for sort_unstable since Rust 1.81, a successor to pdqsort by Lukas Bergdoll and Orson Peters.
example: v.sort_unstable() in current Rust runs ipnsort.

definition: The stable sort Rust has used for slice::sort since Rust 1.81, a merge-based adaptive sort by Orson Peters and Lukas Bergdoll.
example: v.sort() in current Rust runs driftsort.

definition: A quicksort partitioning technique (Edelkamp and Weiß, 2016) that first records which elements are misplaced in small blocks, without branching, and then swaps them. Avoiding unpredictable branches makes it fast for cheap comparisons such as integers.
example: pdqsort uses block partitioning for integer arrays.

definition: An insertion sort that gives up after a small fixed number of element moves. pdqsort uses it when a partition looks already sorted: on sorted data it finishes in linear time, on random data it aborts almost at once.
example: The pdqsort reference implementation allows 8 moves before giving up.

definition: A partition that leaves one side much bigger than the other. Repeated bad partitions make quicksort quadratic, so pdqsort counts them, shuffles a few elements, and falls back to heapsort after about log n of them.
example: Partitioning sorted input around its last element leaves sides of sizes n − 1 and 0.

definition: Timsort's minimum run length: short natural runs are extended to this length with binary insertion sort before merging. CPython picks a value between 32 and 64 for large arrays so the number of runs is close to a power of 2.
example: For a random array of a million elements, most runs are about minrun long.

definition: A stretch of the input that is already in order (ascending, or strictly descending and then reversed) before sorting starts. Timsort finds natural runs and merges them, which is why it is fast on partly sorted data.
example: [1, 4, 7, 9, 8, 5, 2] starts with the natural run 1, 4, 7, 9, followed by the descending run 8, 5, 2.

definition: A Timsort merge mode: when one run keeps supplying the output, it uses an exponential search to find how many elements it can copy in one block, instead of comparing one by one.
example: Galloping finds a 500-element block in about 18 comparisons instead of 500.

definition: The Timsort constant (initially 7) for how many consecutive wins from one run trigger galloping. The threshold adapts: it rises when galloping does not pay off and falls when it does.
example: After 7 elements in a row come from run A, Timsort starts galloping.

definition: Searching a sorted sequence by probing positions 1, 3, 7, 15, … (doubling the step) until overshooting, then binary searching the last gap. It costs about 2 log₂ of the distance to the answer, which is cheap when the answer is near the start or the range is unbounded.
example: Finding position 500 takes about 9 doubling probes and 9 binary search steps.

definition: A search on a sorted array that jumps ahead in fixed blocks of about √n elements until it passes the target, then scans the last block linearly. It takes about √n steps, far more than binary search's log₂ n.
example: On a million sorted items a jump search takes about 1,000 jumps plus up to about 1,000 scans; binary search takes at most 20 probes.

definition: The stack on which Timsort keeps sorted runs waiting to be merged. Its merge rules keep run lengths growing geometrically down the stack, which keeps the stack small and merges balanced.
example: Java's TimSort run stack overflowed on crafted 67-million-element arrays.

definition: Proving mathematically, usually with tool support, that a program meets its specification. In 2015 researchers using the KeY verification tool found that Java's TimSort could violate its own run-stack invariant.
example: The KeY analysis of TimSort produced a crafted input that crashed it.

definition: The Java exception thrown when code accesses an array with an index below 0 or at or beyond its length.
example: Accessing a[5] on a 5-element array throws it.

definition: A Java exception signalling that a method received an invalid argument. TimSort throws it with 'Comparison method violates its general contract!' when it detects an inconsistent comparator.
example: A comparator using a − b with large ints can trigger it.

definition: A Java method that compares two ints and returns a negative number, zero or a positive number without overflow. It is the safe replacement for the a − b comparator.
example: Integer.compare(2000000000, -2000000000) returns a positive number.

definition: Google's JavaScript engine, used in Chrome and Node.js. Since V8 7.0 (2018), Array.prototype.sort uses Timsort.
example: [3, 1, 2].sort() in Chrome runs V8's Timsort.

definition: A runtime for running JavaScript outside the browser, built on the V8 engine.
example: A Node.js server sorting arrays uses V8's Timsort.

definition: Google's mobile operating system. Its Java libraries sort objects with TimSort.
example: Collections.sort in an Android app is a TimSort.

definition: Apple's programming language for iOS, macOS and other platforms. Its standard library sort is a stable Timsort-style merge sort.
example: array.sort() in Swift is stable.

definition: Sorting functions in Go's standard library. sort.Sort and slices.Sort are unstable (pdqsort); sort.Stable and slices.SortStableFunc are stable; sort.Search performs binary search on a predicate.
example: sort.Search(n, func(i int) bool { return a[i] >= x }) finds a lower bound.

definition: Rust's unstable slice sort, faster than the stable sort when the order of equal elements does not matter. It used pdqsort for years and ipnsort since Rust 1.81.
example: v.sort_unstable() sorts a Vec<i32> in place.

definition: Rust's mechanism for stopping a thread when it hits an unrecoverable error, unwinding the stack. Since Rust 1.81 sorting may panic on an inconsistent comparator, but never corrupts memory.
example: Indexing past the end of a Vec panics instead of reading garbage.

definition: The guarantee that a program never reads or writes memory it should not, such as past the end of an array. Violations cause crashes, corruption and security holes; safe Rust guarantees it, C++ does not.
example: std::sort with a bad comparator can write past the vector's end: a memory-safety bug.

definition: The 2019 edition of the ECMAScript (JavaScript) specification, which first required Array.prototype.sort to be stable.
example: Since ES2019, sorting objects by one field keeps ties in their previous order.

definition: Short for JavaScript, the programming language of web browsers.
example: JS engines such as V8 sort with Timsort.

definition: JavaScript's built-in array sort. Without a comparator it converts elements to strings and compares them, so [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9].
example: Use .sort((a, b) => a - b) to sort numbers numerically.

definition: The rules a sort comparator must follow: nothing is less than itself, if a < b then not b < a, 'less than' is transitive, and 'neither is less' (equivalence) is transitive too. Breaking them causes exceptions, undefined behaviour or misordering.
example: a <= b is not a strict weak ordering, because it says a < a.

definition: A relation is irreflexive if nothing is related to itself; for a comparator, compare(a, a) must be false.
example: < is irreflexive; <= is not.

definition: A relation is asymmetric if a related to b means b is not related to a; for a comparator, a < b and b < a cannot both be true.
example: If cmp says 3 < 5 it must not also say 5 < 3.

definition: A relation is transitive if a related to b and b related to c imply a related to c. Sorting relies on 'less than' being transitive.
example: If 1 < 2 and 2 < 3 then 1 < 3.

definition: A function given to a sort that maps each element to the value to sort by. Python calls it once per element (n calls), much cheaper than a comparator called on every comparison.
example: sorted(names, key=str.lower) sorts names case-insensitively.

definition: A Python helper that wraps an old-style comparison function (returning negative, zero or positive) so it can be used as a sort key. Python 3 dropped the cmp argument in favour of key.
example: sorted(xs, key=cmp_to_key(my_cmp)).

definition: The idiom of computing each element's sort key once, sorting the (key, element) pairs, then dropping the keys. Named after Randal Schwartz of the Perl community; Python's key= does it automatically.
example: Sorting files by size with key=os.path.getsize calls getsize once per file.

definition: Ordering sequences by their first element, using the second only to break ties, and so on, like words in a dictionary. Tuple keys in Python and strings are compared this way.

The standard algorithm for shuffling an array uniformly at random in O(n): walk from the end, swapping each position with a random earlier (or same) position. Sorting with a random comparator does not give a uniform shuffle.
example: random.shuffle in Python uses Fisher–Yates.

definition: SQL clauses for paging: LIMIT caps how many rows a query returns and OFFSET skips a number of rows first. Without a total ORDER BY, the rows on each page are not well defined.
example: ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100 returns rows 101 to 150.

definition: A small function written inline without a name, often passed as a sort key or comparator.
example: key=lambda p: p[1] sorts pairs by their second item.

definition: User interface: the screens and controls people use to interact with software, such as a sortable table.
example: Clicking a column header in a UI table re-sorts the rows.

definition: A value that is different for every record, such as a primary key. Appending it to a sort key breaks every tie and makes the order total.
example: ORDER BY created_date, id.

definition: A set of language and regional conventions, such as how text is sorted, how dates are written and which character is the decimal separator.
example: The German and Swedish locales sort 'ä' differently.

definition: The binary search that returns the first index whose element is greater than or equal to x, which is also where x would be inserted to keep the array sorted. It returns len(a) if every element is smaller.
example: In [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8], lower_bound(3) is 1.

definition: The binary search that returns the first index whose element is strictly greater than x. upper_bound(x) − lower_bound(x) counts the copies of x.
example: In [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8], upper_bound(3) is 4, so there are 4 − 1 = 3 threes.

definition: A C++ standard library function returning both lower_bound and upper_bound for a value: the half-open range of elements equal to it.
example: equal_range over [1, 3, 3, 5] for 3 gives positions 1 to 3.

definition: A range that includes both endpoints, written [lo, hi]. A closed-interval binary search loops while lo <= hi and starts with hi = len(a) − 1.
example: [2, 5] contains 2, 3, 4 and 5.

definition: A range that includes its start but not its end, written [lo, hi). Lower-bound binary search uses it: it starts with hi = len(a) and loops while lo < hi.
example: [3, 5) contains 3 and 4 but not 5.

definition: The index halfway between lo and hi that binary search probes next, usually rounded down: (lo + hi) // 2, or lo + (hi − lo) // 2 to avoid overflow.
example: With lo = 4 and hi = 5, the midpoint rounds down to 4.

definition: One look at an element during a search, comparing it with the target. Binary search makes at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes.
example: Searching a million sorted IDs takes at most 20 probes.

definition: A single comparison with three possible outcomes: less than, equal to, or greater than. C's comparators and Java's compareTo return a negative number, zero or a positive number.
example: Comparing 7 with 8 gives 'less'.

definition: A loop whose exit condition never becomes true. In binary search it typically happens when lo = mid makes no progress because mid rounds down to lo.
example: lo = 4, hi = 5: mid = 4, lo = mid = 4, and nothing changes.

definition: A bug where a loop or index is one too many or one too few, such as using len(a) where len(a) − 1 was meant. Binary search is notorious for them.
example: hi = len(a) with while lo <= hi reads one past the end of the array.

definition: A sorted array whose elements have been shifted round by some amount, so it rises, drops once, and rises again. Binary search still works on it for distinct keys, because one half around any midpoint is sorted.
In a rotated sorted array, the position of the minimum, where the values drop. It can be found by binary search comparing a[mid] with a[hi].
example: The rotation point of [15, 18, 22, 3, 6] is index 3.

definition: A yes/no test over an ordered range that is false up to some point and true from then on (or the reverse). Binary search finds the switching point in about log₂ of the range size evaluations.
example: 'Can capacity c ship everything in 5 days?' is monotone in c.

definition: Using binary search over the possible values of an answer, rather than over an array, testing each candidate with a monotone feasibility check.
example: Searching capacities 10 to 55 finds the minimum ship capacity in 5 checks.

definition: A test of whether a candidate answer works, used inside binary search on the answer. It must be monotone for the search to be correct.
example: can_ship(w, days, cap) is the feasibility check for shipping capacity.

term: Ship capacity (binary search on the answer)
definition: In the classic 'ship packages within D days' problem, the most weight the ship can carry in one day. Packages go in order, so a larger capacity never needs more days, which makes 'does capacity c work?' a monotone test that binary search on the answer can use. (Not the same as a dynamic array's capacity.)
example: Weights 1 to 10 within 5 days need a minimum ship capacity of 15.

definition: An algorithm that makes the locally best choice at each step without reconsidering. Greedy methods are fast but give the best answer only for problems with the right structure. Filling each day's ship until the next package would not fit is a greedy check.
example: Greedy packing of [3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 4] with capacity 6 gives 3 days.

definition: The largest whole number whose square is at most n, which can be found by binary search on a monotone predicate.
example: The integer square root of 20 is 4, because 4² = 16 ≤ 20 < 25.

definition: An acceptable error margin for a numerical answer. Binary search on real numbers stops when the interval is narrower than the tolerance, or after an iteration limit.
example: Stop when hi − lo < 10⁻⁹.

definition: An IEEE 754 floating-point value smaller than the smallest normal number, with reduced precision. Near them, simple halving rules for binary search over reals can behave unexpectedly.
example: The smallest positive binary64 subnormal is about 4.9 × 10⁻³²⁴.

definition: A Git command that binary-searches commit history for the commit that introduced a bug, asking you (or a script) whether each tested commit is good or bad.
example: About 10 tests find the bad commit among 1,000 on a linear history.

definition: MySQL's default storage engine. It stores tables in B-tree pages and binary searches the sorted keys inside each page.
example: A primary-key lookup in MySQL walks InnoDB's B-tree pages.

definition: A fixed-size block of storage, often 8 or 16 KB, that databases read and write as a unit. A B-tree page holds many sorted keys, which are binary searched.
example: PostgreSQL uses 8 KB pages; InnoDB uses 16 KB by default.

definition: Java's built-in binary search. It returns the index if found; otherwise −(insertion point) − 1, which is negative even for insertion point 0. It contained the midpoint overflow bug for about nine years.
example: Arrays.binarySearch({10, 20, 30, 40}, 25) returns −3.

definition: The index where a value would be inserted to keep a sorted array sorted: the lower bound of the value.
example: The insertion point of 25 in [10, 20, 30, 40] is 2.

definition: An American computer scientist, author of Programming Pearls. He reported that about 90% of professional programmers he asked wrote binary search with bugs, and with Robert Sedgewick showed that 3-way quicksort is optimal up to a constant factor for inputs with many duplicates.
example: Bentley and McIlroy's 1993 paper 'Engineering a Sort Function' shaped the C library qsort.

definition: A software engineer known for designing parts of the Java platform. In 2006 he revealed the midpoint overflow bug in Java's Arrays.binarySearch.
example: Bloch's 2006 Google blog post was titled 'Nearly All Binary Searches and Mergesorts are Broken'.

definition: A computer scientist and Unix pioneer. His 1999 paper 'A Killer Adversary for Quicksort' showed how to force deterministic quicksorts into quadratic time.
example: McIlroy also invented Unix pipes.

definition: A computer scientist who invented introsort and introselect (1997) and helped create the C++ Standard Template Library.
example: Introsort switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep.

definition: An input at the extremes of what a function accepts, such as an empty array, one element, or a value smaller than everything. Off-by-one bugs hide there.
example: Binary search should be tested on [] and on [x].

definition: The problem of finding the element that would be at index k if the array were sorted, without sorting it. It can be done in O(n) time.
example: The median of 1,001 numbers is the k = 500 smallest (0-based).

definition: An element's position in sorted order. Selection asks for the element of a given rank; 0-based rank 0 is the minimum.
example: In [7, 2, 9], 7 has rank 1.

definition: The value below which a given percentage of observations fall. p99 latency is the response time that 99% of requests beat; p50 is the median.
example: If p99 is 200 ms, one request in a hundred takes longer than 200 ms.

definition: Finding the minimum by pairing elements, keeping each winner and repeating, like a sports knockout. The runner-up must have lost directly to the winner, which finds the second smallest with only about log₂ n extra comparisons.
example: With 1,024 elements, the winner plays 10 rounds, so the second smallest takes 1,032 comparisons in total.

definition: A selection algorithm by David Musser (1997) that runs quickselect and switches to a guaranteed fallback if the range is not shrinking fast enough. With a suitable linear-time fallback it is worst-case O(n). NumPy's np.partition uses it.
example: np.partition(a, k) runs introselect.

definition: A selection algorithm (1975) that picks pivots from a small random sample so the target is very likely between them, needing about n + min(k, n − k) expected comparisons, close to optimal.
example: Finding the median of a million keys takes about 1.5 million comparisons.

definition: C++'s selection function: it rearranges a range so the element at a given position is the one sorted order would put there, with smaller elements before and larger after. The standard requires average linear time.
example: std::nth_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + k, v.end()).

definition: C++'s function that sorts just the k smallest elements of a range into the front, using a heap.
example: std::partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + 10, v.end()) puts the 10 smallest in order at the front.

definition: NumPy's selection function: it places the k-th element where sorting would, smaller ones before it and larger ones after, using introselect with worst-case O(n).
Finding the k largest (or smallest) items. With a heap of size k it takes O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, and works on a stream.
example: The 10 highest-scoring posts out of a million is a top-k query.

definition: The median of a stream, kept up to date as values arrive, usually with two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half.
example: After 5, 15, 1, 3, 8 the running median is 5.

definition: A compact data structure for estimating percentiles of a stream with bounded memory, accurate especially near the extremes such as p99.
example: Monitoring systems use t-digest to report p99 latency.

definition: High Dynamic Range Histogram: a histogram with configurable value range and precision, used to record latency distributions in bounded memory.
example: An HDR Histogram can track latencies from 1 µs to an hour with 3 significant digits.

definition: A source of numbers that look random. Most programs use a pseudorandom generator, which is deterministic from its seed, so an attacker who predicts it can defeat randomised pivots.
example: random.randint(lo, hi) uses Python's Mersenne Twister generator.

definition: Decreasing by a fixed fraction each step, as in n, n/2, n/4, … The total of such a series is bounded by a constant times its first term, which is why quickselect and median of medians are linear.
example: n + n/2 + n/4 + … is less than 2n.

definition: In a size-k heap for top-k, the root holds the worst of the best k seen so far; a new item is admitted only if it beats the root, which is then evicted.
example: Keeping the 3 smallest, a max-heap root of 7 rejects any new value of 7 or more.

definition: A compact probabilistic structure, such as a Count-Min sketch, that estimates how often items occur in a stream using bounded memory.
example: Ranking the most frequent queries in a huge stream can use a frequency sketch.

definition: Whether a sort keeps records with equal keys in their original relative order. A stable sort does; an unstable one may reorder ties. Stability matters when ties are visible to users or when building multi-key sorts from single-key sorts.
example: Sorting orders by date with a stable sort keeps same-day orders in arrival order.

definition: An Apache Spark operation that sorts a distributed data set. It samples the data to choose range boundaries, sends each range to a different machine, and sorts each range locally.
example: rdd.sortBy(lambda r: r.score) sorts records across a cluster.

definition: In PostgreSQL, an old row version left behind by an update or delete that no transaction can see any more. VACUUM reclaims the space.
example: Updating a row 10 times leaves up to 9 dead tuples until VACUUM runs.

definition: The part of a database that decides how to execute a SQL query, for example whether to use an index or sort the rows, based on cost estimates.
example: The planner may read rows in order from a B-tree index instead of sorting them.

definition: A loop that omits its bounds check because it assumes some element (a sentinel or the pivot) will stop it. It is faster, but a comparator that breaks the ordering rules can make it run off the end of the array.
example: libstdc++'s final insertion sort is unguarded after the first block.

definition: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change, for example because of timing. Flaky tests confuse git bisect, which assumes good and bad are reliable.
example: A test that depends on network timing may fail one run in ten.

definition: A Python core developer who designed Timsort for Python in 2002 and documented it in listsort.txt.
example: Timsort is named after Tim Peters.

definition: The designer of pdqsort (2016) and co-designer of Rust's ipnsort and driftsort.
example: pdqsort's paper by Orson Peters appeared on arXiv in 2021.

definition: The design notes for CPython's list sort, written by Tim Peters, describing runs, minrun, galloping and the merge policy.
example: listsort.txt explains why MIN_GALLOP starts at 7.

aliases: Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan
definition: Another name for median of medians, after its 1973 authors Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan: the first selection algorithm proven to run in worst-case linear time.
example: BFPRT splits the input into groups of 5.
